unit.unitOverview: Stop guessing where the object goes. Test a two-word verb with a pronoun and it tells you its kind. visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about small words in the wrong place, and how much they cost.
The reading opens with an email somebody had to write twice.
They wrote that a visit had been put off. It had been called off.
Nine people read it and six kept the afternoon free waiting for a new date that was never coming.
Nothing in that email was bad English. It simply said something else.

Start with the two-word verbs, because there is a real system here that nobody usually tells you.
You have met these twice: Level 2 asked where the object goes, and Unit 1 of this level gave you a set for a life story.
Neither said why some split and some do not.
There are four kinds.
Some take no object. The meeting broke up.
Some split around the object. We carried out the inspection, or we carried the inspection out.
Some never split. We looked into the complaint.
And some have three parts. We ran out of labels.
Here is the problem. With a noun in the sentence, the second and third kinds look identical.
We carried out the inspection. We looked into the complaint. Same shape, both correct.
Now put a pronoun in and watch what happens.
We carried it out. We looked into it.
The first MUST split. The second MUST NOT. Neither has any choice about it.
So the test is short and it never fails. When you meet a new one, try it with it or them straight away.
If the pronoun goes in the middle, the verb splits. If it goes at the end, it does not.
The noun version will never tell you.

The second card is six verbs that appear in almost every procedure and email you will read.
Carry out, set up, take on, put off, call off, sort out.
All six split. All six have a formal single-word twin, which is useful: conduct, establish, recruit, postpone, cancel, resolve.
Knowing both lets you write an email and a report without changing what you mean.
And two of the six are the pair from the reading.
Put off means it is coming, on another day. Call off means it is not coming.
If you do not know which, say you do not know. That is better than guessing and being believed.

The third card is a verb agreement where the meaning and the grammar disagree, and the grammar wins.
Everybody has been told. Not have. Everybody means a great many people and takes a singular verb anyway.
So do nobody, somebody, anybody, something, each and neither.
But then there is a second half that surprises people.
The pronoun that refers back is usually they.
Somebody has left their coat. Everybody should bring their own.
That they is singular, it is standard, and it is centuries old.
So one sentence can quite properly have a singular verb and a they in it at the same time.

The fourth card puts two things side by side that Level 2 taught in different units.
Each other, and themselves.
They blamed each other means A blamed B and B blamed A.
They blamed themselves means each one accepted the fault.
Those are opposite accounts of the same meeting, and both are perfectly good English.
Each other goes across. Themselves goes back. Before you write either, ask which direction you mean.
There is also a third job for the reflexive, which is emphasis. I checked it myself means nobody else did.
And a warning: a few verbs take no reflexive at all. I felt better, never I felt myself better.

The last card is about naming a problem.
You have built abstract nouns four times in this course. What nobody has said is that many of them arrive with a frame attached.
A lack OF supervision. A breakdown IN communication. A shortage OF labels. An increase IN complaints.
And four of them take to plus a plain verb, because the word they came from did too.
A failure to notify. A tendency to run late. A reluctance to put it in writing. An attempt to trace it.
There is a shorter way, which is to chain the nouns. A staff shortage. A communication breakdown.
That is quicker and harder to read, so use it for what your reader already knows, and the longer frame for what is new to them.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: The Email I Had to Write Twice
readings.setting: An office, describing a small disaster
readings.passageScript:
I wrote that the visit had been put off, and it had not. It had been called off.
Two words, one letter apart in my head, and completely different promises.
Nine people read that email and six of them kept the afternoon free for a new date.
Put off means it is coming, later. Called off means it is not coming at all.
I have been more careful with those two ever since.
The second thing I got wrong in the same email was smaller and more interesting.
I wrote that the two departments had blamed themselves.
What had happened was that each had blamed the other, which is blamed each other.
Blamed themselves would have meant both had accepted fault, and nobody had accepted anything.
I did not notice either error. Somebody pointed them out, politely, the next morning.
What I take from it is not that I should write more slowly.
It is that a handful of very ordinary phrases carry a great deal of weight,
and that being wrong about one of them does not look like being wrong.
Both of my sentences were perfectly good English. They simply said something else.

readings.title: Test It With a Pronoun
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passageScript:
Two-word verbs come in four kinds, and most learners meet them one at a time and never see the pattern.
Some take no object at all. The meeting broke up. Sales fell off.
Some take an object and split around it. We carried out the inspection, or we carried the inspection out.
Some take an object and never split. We looked into the complaint.
And some have three parts. We ran out of labels.
With a noun, the first two kinds look identical, and that is the trouble.
We carried out the inspection and we looked into the complaint have exactly the same shape.
Put a pronoun in and the difference appears immediately.
We carried it out. We looked into it.
The first must split. The second must not. Neither has any choice.
So the test is short: whenever you meet a new two-word verb, try it with it or them straight away.
If the pronoun goes in the middle, the verb splits. If it goes at the end, it does not.
The noun version will never tell you, and you will go on not knowing until somebody corrects you.

grammar.title: Carry it out, but look into it: which ones split
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 asked where the object goes. Unit 1 of this level gave you a set.
Neither said WHY some split and some do not, and the answer is short.
There are four kinds, and a pronoun tells you which kind you are holding.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1. NO OBJECT AT ALL
   The meeting broke up. Sales fell off. We set off early.

2. SPLITS, and with a PRONOUN it MUST split
   carry out, set up, take on, put off, call off, sort out, bring up
   We carried out the inspection. / We carried the inspection out.
   We carried it out.  NEVER: we carried out it.

3. NEVER SPLITS
   look into, deal with, come across, look after, rely on
   We looked into the complaint. / We looked into it.
   NEVER: we looked the complaint into.

4. THREE PARTS, and these never split either
   run out of, put up with, look forward to, get on with
   We ran out of labels. We ran out of them.

THE TEST: put a pronoun in.
If it must go in the middle, it is kind 2.
If it must go at the end, it is kind 3 or 4.
The noun version hides the difference. The pronoun exposes it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Which kind is deal with? Try it with a pronoun.
1. Put a noun in first: we dealt with the complaint. That tells you nothing.
2. Now a pronoun. We dealt with it, or we dealt it with?
3. Only the first is possible.
4. The pronoun stays at the end, so it never splits: kind 3.
Answer: deal with never splits. We dealt with it.
Compare carry out: we carried IT out, and never we carried out it.
grammar.commonMistake:
With a noun, kind 2 works both ways, so learners assume kind 3 does too.
No: We looked the complaint into.
Yes: We looked into the complaint.
Test every new one with a pronoun the first time you meet it.
grammar.memoryTip: A noun hides the kind. A pronoun shows it. Always test with a pronoun.

grammar.title: Carried out, set up, put off: the six a workplace runs on
grammar.explanation:
These six appear in almost every procedure, email and report you will read.
All six split. All six have a single-word formal twin, and knowing both
lets you move between an email and a report without changing what you mean.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
carry out  = do, officially      formal twin: conduct, perform
  The inspection was carried out on Tuesday.
set up     = start, establish    formal twin: establish
  They set up a second line in March.
take on    = accept work; employ  formal twin: undertake; recruit
  We took on two more staff in April.
put off    = delay              formal twin: postpone
  The meeting was put off until the 14th.
call off   = cancel             formal twin: cancel
  The visit was called off at short notice.
sort out   = fix, resolve       formal twin: resolve
  Somebody needs to sort out the labelling.

The pair people confuse, and the difference matters:
put off  = it will happen, later.
call off = it will not happen at all.

All six are common in the passive, because a procedure has no I in it.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
The visit is not happening, and no new date will be set. Which verb?
1. Will it happen later? No.
2. put off means delayed to a new date.
3. call off means it is not happening at all.
Answer: The visit was called off.
Writing put off would tell the reader to expect a new date, which is worse
than saying nothing.
grammar.commonMistake:
put off and call off look alike and promise opposite things.
The meeting was put off = it is coming, on another day.
The meeting was called off = it is not coming.
If you do not know which, say so rather than guessing.
grammar.memoryTip: put off delays. call off cancels. Six verbs, six formal twins.

grammar.answerKey:
1. carried out (conduct, perform)  2. set up (establish)
3. took on (recruit, undertake)  4. put off (postpone)
5. called off (cancel)  6. sort out (resolve)
Numbers 4 and 5 are the pair: one promises a new date, the other does not.

grammar.title: Everybody has, and somebody left their coat
grammar.explanation:
Unit 6 taught pronouns pointing back across a sentence.
This card is about a different set, and about one verb agreement that almost
everybody gets wrong at first, because the meaning and the grammar disagree.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE INDEFINITE PRONOUNS take a SINGULAR verb:
Everybody HAS been told.     NOT: everybody have been told.
Nobody KNOWS what happened.
Something IS wrong with the seal.
Neither of them WAS available.
Each of the boxes HAS a label.

Everybody means a lot of people, and it still takes has. The grammar is
singular even though the meaning is plural.

BUT the pronoun that refers back is usually THEY:
Somebody has left THEIR coat.
Everybody should bring THEIR own.
If anyone rings, tell THEM I am out.
That they is singular. It is standard, it is centuries old, and it is what
you use when you do not know who the person is.

So one sentence can have a singular verb and a they in it:
Everybody HAS been told, and THEY all know what to do.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Complete: Somebody ___ (leave) ___ coat in the office.
1. Somebody is an indefinite pronoun, so the verb is singular: has left.
2. Do you know who it was? No.
3. When you do not know, the pronoun that refers back is their.
Answer: Somebody has left their coat in the office.
Singular verb, plural-looking pronoun, and both are correct at once.
grammar.commonMistake:
The verb is where this fails, because the meaning pulls the other way.
No: Everybody have been told.
Yes: Everybody has been told.
Everybody, somebody, nobody, anybody, each and neither: all singular verbs.
grammar.memoryTip: Singular verb, and they to refer back. Both, in the same sentence.

1. has  2. knows  3. was  4. has  5. has left, their  6. them
7. Everybody has been told.
8. Somebody has left their coat. (their is standard and much easier to read)
Numbers 5 and 6 pair a singular verb with they, and both are correct.

grammar.title: They helped each other, or they helped themselves?
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 taught each other in one unit and myself in another, and never put
them side by side. They look similar, they are used in the same shape of
sentence, and they mean completely different things.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
RECIPROCAL — each other, one another. Two or more people, both ways.
They helped each other.      = A helped B, and B helped A.
The two accounts contradict each other.
one another means the same and is slightly more formal.

REFLEXIVE — myself, yourself, themselves. Back onto the same person.
They helped themselves.      = each one helped himself or herself.
She taught herself the system.

Put the two together and hear the difference:
They blamed each other.  = each blamed the other one.
They blamed themselves.  = each blamed himself or herself.
Those are opposite accounts of the same meeting.

REFLEXIVE FOR EMPHASIS, which is a third job:
I checked it myself.  = nobody else did; I did.
The manager himself signed it.

And a warning: some verbs take NO reflexive in English.
I felt better. NOT I felt myself better.
She concentrated. NOT she concentrated herself.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Two departments each said the fault was the other's. Write it.
1. Did each blame itself, or the other one? The other one.
2. Blame going both ways between two parties is reciprocal.
3. Reciprocal is each other.
Answer: The two departments blamed each other.
They blamed themselves would report both departments accepting fault,
which is a very different meeting.
grammar.commonMistake:
Learners use themselves for the reciprocal, and it inverts the meaning.
No: The two accounts contradict themselves. (that says each one is inconsistent)
Yes: The two accounts contradict each other. (they disagree with one another)
Both are real English. Only one of them is what you meant.
grammar.memoryTip: each other goes across. themselves goes back. Ask which direction you mean.

grammar.title: A lack of, a breakdown in: naming a problem
grammar.explanation:
You have built abstract nouns from verbs and adjectives four times now.
What no card has shown is that many of them arrive with a frame attached:
a fixed preposition, and often a fixed article.
Learn the frame and the noun together, or the noun will not work.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
a lack OF          There was a lack of supervision.
a breakdown IN     a breakdown in communication
a shortage OF      a shortage of labels
an increase IN     an increase in complaints
a failure TO       a failure to notify us
a tendency TO      a tendency to run late
a reluctance TO    a reluctance to put it in writing
an attempt TO      an attempt to trace it

Note which ones take TO plus a plain verb: failure, tendency,
reluctance, attempt. Those four came from verbs or adjectives that also
took to, so the frame survived the change.

COMPOUND NOUNS chain in front instead:
a staff shortage        = a shortage of staff
a communication breakdown = a breakdown in communication
a quality control problem  (three nouns, read right to left)

The chain is shorter and harder to read. Use it for what your reader
already knows, and the preposition frame for what is new to them.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Turn this into a noun phrase: Nobody supervised them properly.
1. Find the idea: supervision, or rather the absence of it.
2. Absence takes lack, and lack brings of with it.
3. a lack of supervision.
Answer: There was a lack of supervision.
Or as a chain: a supervision problem. Shorter, vaguer, and only useful if
the reader already knows what the problem was.
grammar.commonMistake:
The frame does not always match the verb the noun came from.
We discussed it, with no preposition, but a discussion ABOUT it.
It failed to arrive, and a failure TO arrive: that one does match.
Check each noun's own frame rather than assuming it inherited one.
grammar.memoryTip: Learn the noun with its preposition. Chain nouns only for what the reader already knows.

assignments.title: The email, and the error that reads as correct
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write an internal email with four numbered items, in about 150 words.
Use at least six two-word verbs, and put a pronoun after three of them so the
reader can see which kind they are.
One item must say what has been put off and make clear it has not been called off.
Use at least two nouns with their own preposition, and one singular they.
Part two. Now write two sentences that are perfectly good English and say something
you did NOT mean: one swapping put off for call off, and one swapping each other
for themselves.
Beside each, write what a reader would do as a result.
Part three. Write four sentences about your own work using these adjectives, each
with the right form after it: reluctant, liable, prone, eager.
